clinical_record:
An 8-year-old girl weighing 44.5 kg with no significant medical history presented with a 1-week history of progressive abdominal pain, distension, nausea, and vomiting. Physical examination revealed notable abdominal distension without guarding or rebound. Initial abdominal ultrasonography showed a 17 × 9 cm mixed solid and cystic mass occupying the right hepatic lobe with compression of the inferior vena cava (IVC). By hospital day 7, worsening abdominal distension and concern for abdominal compartment syndrome prompted percutaneous biopsy of the mass and placement of a drain. Over the next several days, persistent sanguineous output from the drain led to anemia and concern for hemorrhage. Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated an infrarenal IVC thrombus and a near-occlusive embolus in the left pulmonary artery. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed compression of the distal IVC at its junction with the right atrium, with otherwise normal biventricular function and no evidence of elevated right heart pressures.

A 22-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of generalized painful fluid‐filled skin lesions, 7 days of yellow scleral discoloration, and 1 month of fever following removal of a tibial implant. Two years earlier, he had sustained a tibial fracture treated with internal fixation. After implant removal, he developed a surgical-site infection and persistent fever; he initially took paracetamol without relief, then obtained ciprofloxacin over the counter. Two days after starting ciprofloxacin, he developed generalized pruritus that progressed to fluid-filled rashes. He denied angioedema, dyspnea, abdominal distention, lower-limb swelling, hematemesis, melena, altered sensorium, alcohol use, or immunocompromise.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. He had icterus but no pallor, clubbing, cyanosis, lymphadenopathy, or dehydration. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Dermatologic examination showed multiple generalized vesicles and bullae with non-hemorrhagic crusts over the trunk and extremities (palms and soles spared). Lesions were tender, with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Mucosal findings included hemorrhagic lip crusts and penile erosion.

A 39-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of persistent fever, night sweats, a 15-kg weight loss, decreased appetite, dry cough, and shortness of breath. He had no significant medical history, no recent travel, and no known sick contacts, but lived in close quarters with 13 other inmates. On examination, his heart rate was elevated, blood pressure was low but responsive to fluids, and he had fine tremors. Laboratory studies showed hyponatremia, elevated liver enzymes (AST, ALT, ALP), and raised inflammatory markers. Anteroposterior chest radiography revealed numerous bilateral tiny nodules throughout both lung fields. Contrast CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis confirmed innumerable widespread pulmonary nodules, a few cavitary lesions, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Because of his headache, an MRI of the brain was obtained, which demonstrated vasogenic edema in the left posterior insula and temporoparietal cortex, intraparenchymal hemorrhage in the same region, and overlying leptomeningeal enhancement—findings consistent with hemorrhagic meningoencephalitis.

A 53-year-old Hispanic man presented with painful left lower-extremity swelling and erythema. Six months earlier, incidentally noted bilateral adrenal and periaortic retroperitoneal masses were not further evaluated. He reported intermittent fevers, episodic night sweats, decreased appetite, and palpitations. He denied trauma or injury to the leg. On examination, the left calf had ill-defined, warm, confluent erythema, edema, and tender induration. Laboratory studies showed mild lymphocytopenia, moderate anemia, elevated creatine kinase, elevated aldolase, and elevated lactate dehydrogenase; peripheral-blood flow cytometry was unremarkable. CT and MRI of the leg revealed gastrocnemius myositis, extensive subcutaneous and superficial myofascial edema, and popliteal lymphadenopathy without evident lymphatic obstruction. He was started on intravenous ceftriaxone for presumed cellulitis and pyomyositis but did not improve. A punch biopsy of skin from the lower leg showed a sparse perivascular and interstitial infiltrate of enlarged atypical mononuclear cells in the reticular dermis and subcutis, not consistent with cellulitis.

clinical_record:
A 46-year-old woman presented with right flank pain, dysuria, and hematuria. Her past medical history was notable for an abdominal hysterectomy 15 years earlier. General and pelvic examinations were unremarkable. Urinalysis showed 6–8 red blood cells and 4–6 pus cells per high-power field but no other abnormalities.

An ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a focal hypoechoic polypoidal lesion measuring 3.4 × 2.8 cm along the anterosuperior wall of the urinary bladder, containing tiny hyperechoic foci; the outline of the adjacent bladder wall appeared indistinct. The uterus was not visualized; a cystic area was noted in the left adnexa, and both ovaries were not seen.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed a well-defined soft-tissue–density lesion with calcific specks along the anterosuperior bladder wall that demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement in the early arterial and venous phases. The intraluminal component merged with the bladder wall, causing minimal localized wall thickening; the rest of the bladder wall was normal. Additional findings included a right calyceal calculus with mild pelvicalyceal dilatation, a simple right renal cyst, no pelvic lymphadenopathy, and left hydrosalpinx.

On imaging, possibilities such as endometriosis, a mucosal neoplastic lesion, or a granulomatous lesion of the urinary bladder were considered.

clinical_record:
An 83-year-old man presented with 6 months of progressive right mandibular pain radiating to the zygomatic and mastoid regions, requiring oxycodone, paracetamol, and ketorolac for relief. An empirical course of prednisone (50 mg per day) for presumed trigeminal neuralgia provided no benefit. Contrast-enhanced maxillofacial CT showed enlargement of the right sphenoid sinus with overdevelopment and opacity of the lateral recess, bone thickening and sclerosis of the sphenoid walls, pterygoid process, and orbital apex, and focal interruption of the foramen rotundum and lateral recess wall. Gadolinium-enhanced MRI demonstrated soft tissue protruding through a breach in the lateral recess wall of the sphenoid sinus, invading the right internal pterygoid muscles, masticatory and pterygopalatine fossae, and infiltrating the V2 and V3 trigeminal branches; intracranial extension into the cavernous sinus surrounded the Gasserian ganglion, with the cavernous carotid artery patent. T2-weighted images showed a markedly hypointense signal in the lateral recess with peripheral mucosal inflammation. Endoscopic evaluation revealed purulent discharge in the sphenoethmoidal recess. The patient underwent right endoscopic sinus surgery: after middle turbinectomy, the sphenoid ostium was obstructed by a pyocele, which was marsupialized and drained; samples of the lesion and surrounding mucosa were sent for bacteriological and histopathological examination. The maxillary and ethmoid sinuses were then opened, the breach in the posterior-lateral sphenoid wall was repaired with mucoperiosteum, and a Merocel sponge was placed. He was discharged after 2 days without complications. Histopathology was negative for hyphae and neoplastic cells, and cultures grew no bacteria or fungi. One month after surgery, follow-up MRI confirmed persistent inflammation of the sphenoid sinus, skull base, and pterygoid fossa. A consultation with an infectious diseases specialist was sought.

A 74-year-old right-handed woman was brought to the psychiatry clinic with a 5-month history of abrupt onset of disorganized speech, severe anxiety, and self-harm behaviors that began after a family trip. Her speech was rapid, fluent, and nonsensical—exemplified by the phrase “Our neighbor has gone to the cobbler to buy Ghormeh Sabzi”—consistent with Wernicke’s aphasia. Over the ensuing months, she developed agitation, persecutory delusions, visual and auditory hallucinations, urinary and fecal incontinence, and a persistent urge to flee her home.

Her psychiatric history included a 10-year history of depression treated with sertraline. There was no prior cognitive impairment or neurological disease. On examination, she was disoriented to time, demonstrated anomia, and had marked perseveration on the Clock Drawing Test, impaired performance on Luria’s three-step test, and defective crossed-pentagon drawing. Cognitive testing revealed an MMSE score of 2/30 and an ACE-R score of 2/100, likely confounded by comprehension deficits.

An initial brain MRI performed 2 months after symptom onset was reported as normal. She was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease and started on memantine and quetiapine, without clinical improvement. Because of the acute presentation and prominent frontal and temporal features, she was referred to neurology for further assessment.
